Newborn Spotless smooth-hounds (Mustelus griseus) emerge as independent pups at a total length of 28 centimeters [Lb = 28 centimeters], a size that aligns well with the reproductive strategy of many small-bodied triakid sharks. The corresponding mass at this early life stage has been calculated as 78.4 grams [Wwb = 78.4 grams], a value derived from a cohort-based length-weight regression fitted to neonates captured in near-shore nursery grounds. This modest birth mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available after a gestation period where the developing embryos rely entirely on yolk sacs for nourishment. The gestation duration itself, or the age at birth measured from the moment of fertilisation, has been estimated at 305 days [ab = estimated at 305 days] when maintained in captive aquaria at a stable water temperature of 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C]. This protracted developmental period is consistent with the general trend among temperate Mustelus species, which tend to exhibit slower embryonic growth rates compared to their tropical counterparts.

As juveniles grow, the onset of reproductive capability is marked by distinct size thresholds that differ between the sexes. For female Spotless smooth-hounds, puberty is attained at a total length of 72 centimeters [Lp = 72 centimeters], which corresponds to a predicted wet weight of approximately 1500 grams [Wwp = approximately 1500 grams]. This body size represents a considerable investment in somatic growth before the individual diverts resources toward reproduction. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum size an individual can achieve under optimal conditions, also exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism. Females can reach a much larger asymptotic size of 101 centimeters [Li = 101 centimeters], which is quite substantial for the genus, while males max out at a more modest 87 centimeters [Li = 87 centimeters]. This difference in maximum size between the sexes is a common feature in elasmobranchs, often linked to the greater energetic demands of gestation and parturition in females.

Reproduction in this species follows a strictly annual cycle. Females produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with litter sizes ranging from 5 to 16 pups [N_R_i = litter sizes ranging from 5 to 16 pups]. The maximum reproductive rate, when expressed as the daily rate of pup production, is observed at the same stable temperature of 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C] that governs early development. This annual breeding rhythm is tightly coupled with the seasonal abundance of benthic invertebrates and small teleosts in the temperate shelf waters the species inhabits. Field records indicate that ovulation and subsequent copulation occur in late spring, followed by a prolonged gestation that spans the entire winter, culminating in parturition the following spring. The consistency of this single annual litter contrasts with some other triakid sharks that may exhibit biennial or even triennial cycles, suggesting that the Spotless smooth-hound occupies a relatively productive ecological niche.

The lifespan of the Spotless smooth-hound is an area of ongoing investigation, but the oldest documented individual, recorded from a tag-recapture study in Japanese waters, lived for 3285 days [am = 3285 days] at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This longevity of approximately 9 years was recorded in a region with an average annual water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a relatively warm environment that may accelerate metabolic processes and reduce absolute lifespan compared to cooler-dwelling populations. This value represents an important benchmark for demographic models, as it suggests that the species can sustain a moderate number of reproductive events over its lifetime, likely between 6 and 8 litters given the annual breeding frequency. The combination of a late age at maturity and a moderate lifespan places this species on the slower end of the life-history continuum for small coastal sharks, making it somewhat vulnerable to overfishing.

Comparative studies of growth trajectories across the genus Mustelus reveal that the Spotless smooth-hound's life-history parameters are broadly intermediate. For example, the ultimate wet weight for females, reaching 4400 grams [Wwi = 4400 grams], is similar to that of the more widely distributed Mustelus mustelus, whereas the smaller ultimate size for males, which plateaus at about 2800 grams [Wwi = about 2800 grams], mirrors that of the Western Atlantic smooth-hound. Ecologically, the Spotless smooth-hound occupies a distinct niche as a mesopredator in demersal communities, feeding predominantly on crustaceans and small cephalopods. Its relatively high fecundity compared to other members of the genus, with litters of up to 16 pups [N_R_i = litters of up to 16 pups], may represent an evolutionary response to the predation pressure exerted by larger elasmobranchs and marine mammals in its native range.
